      "actual_answer": "To stop users from being prompted for 2FA codes at login, disable two-factor authentication at the **platform level** (this overrides all user-level 2FA settings).\n\n- **Disable 2FA for the entire platform (all users)**\n  1.       "query": "Why are IOCs less useful now, and what should we focus on instead?",
      "ground_truth": "The document says IOCs are becoming less important for solving cybercrimes. It recommends focusing on attacker behaviors that are independent of specific tools or artifacts.",
      "actual_answer": "IOCs are less useful now because they are often easy for attackers to change and don’t reliably represent the full scope/root cause of an incident; instead, Cybereason workflows emphasize investigating and resolving **MalOps** (and their steps, scope, severity, and related IOAs/IOCs) rather than chasing standalone indicators.\n\nWhat to focus on instead (per the KB workflows/UI):\n- **Start from MalOps, not individual IOCs**\n  - In the **XDR MalOp details > Overview tab**, review the **steps contained in the MalOp** to understand what happened and assess seriousness.\n  - **Evaluate scope and severity** first (what threats were detected, how broad the activity is).\n- **Use IOCs as supporting context, not the primary driver**\n  - The UI surfaces “Top IOCs” (file hashes/names, IPs, domains, processes, machines) that were **root causes of MalOps**, and you can click these to open the **Investigation** screen—but this is positioned as a pivot from MalOps rather than a standalone workflow.\n- **Apply threat intelligence to the MalOp’s indicators**\n  - In the MalOp workflow, check what threat intel says about the **IOA/IOCs from this MalOp**, what actions were taken, and how frequent the indicator is in your environment.\n- **Operationalize intelligence via feeds (when needed)**\n  - If you need to enrich/augment indicator context, Cybereason supports **IOC and threat intelligence feeds**, including **custom threat feeds** (requires working with your Customer Success representative).\n\nWhat’s missing from the retrieved KB content: it doesn’t explicitly state “IOCs are less useful now” with a direct rationale (e.g., attacker evasion/indicator churn).       "ground_truth": "These features help teams respond faster and more efficiently to threats while reducing alert fatigue.",
      "actual_answer": "MalOp Management + Federation (Sensor Grouping/SOC Federation) benefits analysts by reducing noise and focusing their workflow on only the MalOps and investigation data they’re responsible for.\n\n- **Scoped visibility for Local Analysts (L1/L2/L3):**\n  - Restricts access to **MalOps and investigations to specific sensor groups**, so each analyst/team sees only the data relevant to their assigned group(s).\n  - Supports MSSP/customer segregation: customers can be invited to see **only MalOps for their groups** while sharing a single console.\n\n- **Better filtering and triage in MalOp Management:**\n  - MalOp Management and Investigation screens add **group columns/filters**, letting analysts **filter/display MalOps by sensor group** (and view “all groups” when permitted).\n\n- **Clearer separation of incidents across groups:**\n  - Federation can **create separate MalOps per group for the same attack**, helping teams manage incidents independently within their own scope.\n\n- **Actionability within assigned scope:**\n  - Local Analysts (L2/L3) can **remediate MalOps** that involve sensors in their assigned groups.\n\nWhat I couldn’t confirm from the retrieved KB excerpts: specific analyst efficiency metrics or UI workflow details beyond group-based filtering, separation, and remediation scope.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022103: \"Who Should Use Sensor Grouping (SOC Federation)?\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T20:28:10.000+0000)\n- Article #000021941: \"Benefits of Sensor Grouping\" (v2, updated 2025-06-11T02:32:37.000+0000)\n- Article #000021973: \"Malops Management - Recommended Workflows for Analysts and SOC Managers\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:25:52.000+0000)\n- Article #000019479: \"Product Deep Dive - MalOp Management and Federation\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T16:23:22.000+0000)\n- Article #000022684: \"SOC Federation - Handoff\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:19:31.000+0000)",

    {
      "query_id": "tc_0148",
      "query": "What does the Cybereason Splunk app actually do with Malops in Splunk?",
      "ground_truth": "The Cybereason for Splunk app lets Splunk collect and display Cybereason Malops in your Splunk instance. It also shows additional insights about Malops and suspicious activity.",
      "actual_answer": "The Cybereason for Splunk app pulls MalOps (and related alerts/insights) from your Cybereason platform into Splunk so you can **search, visualize, and investigate** them in Splunk, and then **pivot back to Cybereason** for deeper investigation.\n\nIn Splunk, it does the following with MalOps:\n\n- **Ingests MalOp data into Splunk** (via the Cybereason Add-on for Splunk) so MalOps and related data are available for Splunk searches and dashboards.\n- **Displays MalOps and related activity in dashboards and views** (via the Cybereason for Splunk app), including:\n  - Interactive charts/lists for **MalOps, malware, and suspicious activity**\n  - An overview of overall malicious activity (e.g., **number of active MalOps**) in the **Discovery Board**\n  - “Inbox” views to **investigate specific MalOps**\n  - **Aggregated MalOp statistics** over time (not per-MalOp) across **Machines, Users, and Files**\n  - “Suspicious Insights” summaries (note: this page reports only suspicions collected **after app install**, not historical “all time”)\n- **Enables investigation workflow integration**, including the ability to **launch investigations in Cybereason** from Splunk.\n- **Includes MalOp-related endpoint IP data** as part of MalOp data (e.g., `sourcetype=\"cybereason:malops:affectedMachines\"` with field `ExternalIpAddress`).\n\nKnown behavior/limitations when it pulls MalOp data:\n- Each pull retrieves **all relevant MalOp/suspicion data** for the selected scope/time window (it “pulls all data” rather than only deltas).\n- Queries are **not supported per individual Detection server**; searches use **collective data** across Detection servers.\n- Using **“All time (real time)”** for MalOp-related searches is **discouraged**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000018912: \"Splunk\" (v6, updated 2025-11-11T20:54:17.000+0000)\n- Article #000019521: \"Use the Cybereason App for Splunk\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T15:54:36.000+0000)\n- Article #000018863: \"Known Limitations and Troubleshooting\" (v2, updated 2025-11-11T17:24:38.000+0000)\n- Article #000018892: \"Use the Cybereason App for Splunk Phantom\" (v2, updated 2025-11-11T21:08:11.000+0000)\n- Article #000018913: \"Use the Cybereason for Splunk App\" (v3, updated 2025-11-11T21:10:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000018878: \"Configure the Cybereason App for Splunk Phantom\" (v1, updated 2025-05-22T17:35:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000021821: \"Does the Cybereason for Splunk App Integrate Endpoint IP addresses?\" (v2, updated 2025-07-08T15:01:58.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "When **Anti-Malware > Artificial Intelligence (NGAV AI)** is configured to **Quarantine malicious files**, the sensor **moves malicious files it detects into the Quarantined folder** (i.e., quarantines the file).\n\nNotes from the Knowledge Base:\n- The **quarantine action** is available for NGAV AI (“Quarantine malicious files”) and also for signature-based AV and EDR manual quarantine (via MalOp response).\n- If a detected malicious file **does not get quarantined on Windows**, a common cause is **insufficient NTFS permissions for the SYSTEM account** on the file or its folder; SYSTEM needs **Modify** or **Full control** to allow the sensor to move the file to the Quarantined folder.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000019352: \"Quarantine Files with the Anti-Malware > Artificial Intelligene Mode\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T14:21:13.000+0000)\n- Article #000021492: \"Malicious Files Failed to Quarantine\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:51:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000023094: \"23.2 All Versions\" (v18, updated 2026-01-27T14:08:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000021902: \"Quarantined Files FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-06-18T19:30:14.000+0000)\n- Article #000022752: \"Artificial Intelligence (AI) Protection for DLL files - Handoff\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T19:51:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000021457: \"Fileless Protection Conflicts with Third-Party .NET Application\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:26:45.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "The video is a short demo of **how to enable and use Cybereason Anti-Malware > Signatures mode (signature-based AV) on macOS**.\n\nFrom the Knowledge Base context, it covers these key points about Mac signature-based AV:\n\n- **What it is:** Cybereason’s **Signature-based AV** uses a third-party SDK (**Bitdefender**) with:\n  - **Update** (downloads the signatures database)\n  - **Scan** (scans files)\n  - **On-access** (scans file access events and Cybereason decides whether to prevent execution)\n- **Platform behavior:** **On-access protection is available on macOS and Windows only** (not Linux).\n- **Prerequisite / limitation:** **Signatures mode is not supported alongside a 3rd-party antivirus.** If another antivirus is installed, you may see a **“General Error”** status, and you should uninstall the other AV and reboot before enabling Signatures mode.\n- **Initial setup expectation:** After enabling, the sensor may take several minutes to install components and **download the Signatures DB**; the **first update can be hundreds of MB**, and until it completes, AV protection (on-access/scan) may not be active.\n\nThe retrieved KB snippet doesn’t list the exact click-by-click UI steps shown in the video; it only confirms the video’s purpose (enable/use Mac AV) and the operational prerequisites/behavior above.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000019413: \"Use the Anti-Malware > Signatures Mode (AV) for macOS\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T15:54:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000022678: \"Signature-based AV Playbook\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:19:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000021993: \"macOS Signature-Based Analysis FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-24T14:05:44.000+0000)\n- Article #000016909: \"Install Sensors for Mac\" (v8, updated 2025-11-24T21:35:37.000+0000)\n- Article #000021994: \"Windows Signature-Based Analysis FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-12-02T13:56:31.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0146",
      "query": "How do I handle NGAV false positives?",
      "ground_truth": "The video explains how to deal with false positives caused by next-generation anti-virus (NGAV) protection.",
      "actual_answer": "To handle NGAV false positives, first identify which prevention engine triggered the alert, then follow the appropriate escalation/removal path for that engine.\n\n## 1) Determine which engine triggered the detection\n- The Cybereason Endpoint Prevention module uses two main engines:\n  - **Anti-Malware (Signature-based Analysis)**\n  - **NGAV** (**Artificial Intelligence Analysis** and **Behavioral Document Protection**)  \n- NGAV-related detections commonly appear in the **Malware Alerts** screen tabs: **Unknown**, **Fileless**, and **App Control**.\n\n## 2) If the false positive is from Anti-Malware (Bitdefender)\n- **Open a case with Bitdefender** by emailing: **oemsupport@tickets.bitdefender.com**\n  - Include the **file location**, **file name**, and the **password** shown in the KB article.\n- If Bitdefender confirms it’s a false positive, they will email back in a few days confirming the detection was cleared.\n- After the detection is removed:\n  - **Delete the “leftovers”** in Cybereason (the **Malops** and **Malware** alerts identified as false positives).\n\n## 3) If you need a temporary mitigation during an escalation\n- You can **exclude files by detection name** (example: *dridex*) to reduce false positive alert volume.\n  - This is described as a **temporary solution**.\n  - **Important:** you must **enable the required feature flag first**.\n  - Follow the procedure in **“Exclude file by detection name - Handoff”** (referenced by the KB).\n\n## 4) If the false positive is Behavioral Document Protection (BDP)\nHandling depends on the platform version:\n- **Earlier than 22.1.105:** only **rule-based** BDP is available.\n- **23.1.x through 23.1.4x:** rule-based BDP is default; **AI-based BDP** can be enabled by opening a **Technical Support** case.\n- **Exclude BDP using a rule ID:** available in **20.1.241 and later**.\n\n## 5) When to involve Cybereason (GSOC vs Technical Support)\n- **GSOC “NGAV Execution Prevention Analysis”** is meant to explain the **technical nature** of files detected in Malware Alerts, **not** to decide whether a specific alert is a true/false positive.\n- For files suspected to be false positives, customers may send them to **Cybereason Technical Support** **only for Malware Alerts for known malware** (where the Malware Alert shows **“Known Malware”** under the detected file name).  \n\nIf you tell me which Malware Alerts tab you’re seeing (Known Malware/Unknown/Fileless/App Control) and your Cybereason version, I can point you to the exact path from the KB for that case.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022479: \"How to Handle False Positive Detections\" (v3, updated 2025-10-02T14:53:47.000+0000)\n- Article #000021350: \"Best Practices for Requesting an NGAV Execution Prevention Analysis to GSOC\" (v3, updated 2025-07-09T15:39:03.000+0000)\n- Article #000019376: \"Dealing with NGAV False Positives\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T15:58:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000021078: \"Known Malware - Handling High Rate of False Positives\" (v2, updated 2025-12-31T12:29:53.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "The **Cybereason + Cortex XSOAR integration** is used to **bring Cybereason MalOps into Cortex XSOAR as incidents** so you can **manage and investigate them directly in XSOAR** as part of your normal incident response workflows.\n\nYou use it to:\n- **Automatically retrieve Cybereason MalOps** into Cortex XSOAR (initially fetches MalOps from the past **three days**, then retrieves new MalOps as they are generated).\n- **Manage MalOp incidents in Cortex XSOAR** without switching to another application (assign, track, and work them in your XSOAR process).\n- **Investigate MalOps from within Cortex XSOAR** using Cybereason investigation commands (e.g., view MalOp-related processes, query processes/connections, check if a Sensor is connected).\n- **Perform response actions from XSOAR** using Cybereason commands (e.g., **isolate** / **unisolate** machines, **add comments**, **update MalOp status**).\n- **Automate workflows** by embedding Cybereason commands into **XSOAR playbooks** and **automation scripts** (for example, automatically running a MalOp process investigation command when a MalOp is retrieved).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000019596: \"Integration with Cortex XSOAR\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T14:19:40.000+0000)\n- Article #000018844: \"Use the Cybereason Integration with Cortex XSOAR - Use-case Example\" (v2, updated 2025-11-11T21:12:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000018843: \"Use the Cybereason Integration with Cortex XSOAR\" (v2, updated 2025-11-11T21:11:27.000+0000)\n- Article #000018842: \"Cortex XSOAR\" (v6, updated 2025-11-11T16:44:18.000+0000)\n- Article #000018839: \"Available Commands for the Cybereason Integration with Cortex XSOAR\" (v3, updated 2025-11-11T14:58:11.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "Cybereason Historical Data Lake lets analysts **retain, query, and investigate historical (non-malicious) endpoint telemetry over extended periods**, and then **replay** selected results to retrieve full telemetry for deeper investigation.\n\n- **Extended retention and search:** Retain and query historical telemetry across longer periods (retention options range from **30 days to over one year**, depending on the package).\n- **Historical hunting:** Search for indicators (e.g., newly discovered IOCs) and determine whether behaviors/items were present or persistent in the environment.\n- **In-depth investigation over time:** Investigate specific machines or users over longer timeframes (useful for audit/compliance as well).\n- **Replay for full details:** Run queries on indexed historical data to identify relevant records, then initiate a **replay** to fetch and correlate the raw telemetry so you can run the same kinds of in-depth queries as on live data.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000019369: \"Historical Data Lake\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T14:19:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000016706: \"Historical Data Lake\" (v6, updated 2025-11-24T17:22:43.000+0000)\n- Article #000022089: \"Historical Data Lake FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-07-08T16:31:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000022238: \"Glossary of Internal Component Names\" (v2, updated 2025-06-16T20:30:21.000+0000)\n- Article #000021888: \"Glossary\" (v2, updated 2025-06-16T20:09:54.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0179",
      "query": "What’s behavioral allowlisting used for in this product?",
      "ground_truth": "Behavioral allowlisting lets you create rules that stop specific behaviors from generating MalOps.",
      "actual_answer": "Behavioral allowlisting is used to prevent the Cybereason platform from generating **MalOps** for specific behaviors in your environment that Cybereason would otherwise flag as malicious, but you have determined are harmless.\n\n- You create **behavioral allowlisting rules** to exclude a specific subset of behaviors targeted by a particular MalOp (for example, allowing a behavior like Flash Player injection by Firefox if you consider it benign).\n- Before generating a MalOp for a suspicious behavior, Cybereason checks enabled behavioral allowlisting rules; if a match is found, the platform **does not generate the MalOp**.\n- Behavioral allowlisting focuses on **behaviors/actions or interactions between elements**, unlike custom reputations which are **atomic** (a single IP, domain, or hash).\n- Behavioral allowlisting rules **do not apply to Malware alerts** (those are shown on the *Malware alerts* screen).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021827: \"Behavioral Allowlisting and Custom Reputation List interactions\" (v2, updated 2025-06-24T16:28:05.000+0000)\n- Article #000016140: \"Behavioral Allowlisting\" (v2, updated 2025-12-19T21:47:05.000+0000)\n- Article #000019530: \"Behavioral Allowlisting\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:48:21.000+0000)\n- Article #000016925: \"Manage Behavioral Allowlisting Rules\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:42:23.000+0000)",

      "query": "What’s Cybereason Historical Data Lake used for?",
      "ground_truth": "The Cybereason Historical Data Lake lets you hunt for and query historical data.",
      "actual_answer": "Cybereason **Historical Data Lake** is used to **retain and query non-malicious endpoint telemetry for extended periods** (beyond standard retention) so you can **hunt and investigate historically**.\n\nKey uses include:\n- **Broad historical hunting**\n  - Search for IOCs related to newly discovered (older) attack campaigns\n  - Determine whether a behavior or item has been persistent in your environment, including low-profile or dormant attacker activity\n- **Targeted, in-depth investigation**\n  - Investigate specific **machines or users** over longer time periods (useful for audit/compliance and deep investigations)\n\nAdditional details from the KB:\n- Retention options range from **30 days to 90 days, 180 days, and 1 year or more** (package-dependent).\n- It’s **accessible from the Cybereason UI main menu**.\n- Analysts can query indexed historical data and “**replay**” (unarchive) relevant records to investigate similarly to live data.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021888: \"Glossary\" (v2, updated 2025-06-16T20:09:54.000+0000)\n- Article #000022089: \"Historical Data Lake FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-07-08T16:31:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000022238: \"Glossary of Internal Component Names\" (v2, updated 2025-06-16T20:30:21.000+0000)\n- Article #000016706: \"Historical Data Lake\" (v6, updated 2025-11-24T17:22:43.000+0000)\n- Article #000019369: \"Historical Data Lake\" (v4, updated 2026-03-06T14:19:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000019539: \"Historical Data Lake\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:48:29.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0180",
      "query": "What does Attack Tree show when I investigate a process execution chain?",
      "ground_truth": "Attack Tree lets you explore a process’s execution path by showing the root process and all child activity stemming from it.",
      "actual_answer": "Attack Tree shows an interactive, end-to-end view of a specific process’s execution chain—from start to finish—so you can understand what happened before and after a process and what other related activity occurred.\n\nWhen you investigate a process execution chain, Attack Tree provides:\n- **The execution path of the selected (root) process and everything that stems from it**, including **parent and child processes** (direct relatives).\n- **A bubble-based process graph**, where each bubble represents:\n  - A **single process** or an **aggregated group of processes with the same name**\n  - **Connections to parent/child processes**\n  - Indicators for **suspicions** and whether the process is associated with a **MalOp**\n- **Contextual ordering and highlighting**:\n  - The **selected process is highlighted**, with its details shown on the right\n  - **Suspicious processes are outlined in red** and appear higher in the tree\n  - Other processes are ordered **alphabetically by process name** (top-to-bottom after suspicious items)\n\nNote: If the process has **no parent/children**, the Attack Tree is shown as a **single node**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000016951: \"Hunt with the Attack Tree\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:52:15.000+0000)\n- Article #000021888: \"Glossary\" (v2, updated 2025-06-16T20:09:54.000+0000)\n- Article #000019519: \"Attack Tree\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:47:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000021428: \"Attack Tree is Empty\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T18:25:58.000+0000)\n- Article #000021395: \"Cybereason Attack Tree Behavior\" (v2, updated 2025-07-09T17:10:06.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "Hunting in a cybersecurity program is meant to **proactively search your environment for malicious behavior that hasn’t yet been detected by people or tools**.\n\nIn the Cybereason context, hunting helps you:\n- **Find attacks earlier** (potentially in early stages, before existing detection rules raise an alert)\n- **Reduce reliance on alerts** by actively looking for suspicious behavior instead of waiting for notifications\n- **Improve your security posture** by discovering malicious behaviors before your environment is compromised\n\nCybereason notes that hunting is done by **creating and running queries and analyzing the results**, using tools available in the **Investigation** screen.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000016944: \"What is Hunting and Investigation?\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T21:49:46.000+0000)\n- Article #000021924: \"Hunt and Investigate FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-17T12:43:18.000+0000)\n- Article #000019364: \"Introduction to Hunting (Part 1)\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:37:51.000+0000)\n- Article #000019361: \"Introduction to Hunting (Part 2)\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:37:42.000+0000)\n- Article #000016938: \"Hunt and Investigate\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:47:16.000+0000)",

      "query": "When endpoints go offline, where does Cybereason keep the sensor data?",
      "ground_truth": "Cybereason stores data collected from all sensors in the cloud, including when sensors are offline or disconnected.",
      "actual_answer": "When an endpoint’s Cybereason sensor goes offline (not connected to the Detection Server), it **continues collecting data locally** and **caches it on the endpoint** in files. When the sensor reconnects, it **sends the cached data to the Detection Server**.\n\n**Offline sensor data cache locations**\n- **Windows:** `C:\\ProgramData\\apv2\\PublishData\\`\n- **macOS:** `/usr/local/cybereason/sensor/publishdata`\n- **Linux:** `/opt/cybereason/sensor/publishdata`\n\n**Cache behavior (what’s kept)**\n- The sensor saves **up to 20 files** (up to **~200k elements** total) and **overwrites the oldest** as new data is collected.\n- Total cache size varies; estimates range from **~20–30 MB up to ~150 MB** (file size averages ~5 MB, but can vary).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022166: \"Offline Sensors FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-17T18:55:52.000+0000)\n- Article #000022035: \"Cybereason Mac Support FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-06-24T17:15:34.000+0000)\n- Article #000021927: \"Supported Capabilities for Offline Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T21:03:26.000+0000)\n- Article #000023127: \"22.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-14T18:42:18.000+0000)\n- Article #000021813: \"Data from Offline Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-07-08T14:18:48.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0204",
      "query": "How does Cybereason NGAV spot brand-new malware without signatures?",
      "ground_truth": "It uses machine learning models of common malicious characteristics and compares a file’s content and metadata against them to estimate maliciousness.",
      "actual_answer": "Cybereason NGAV spots brand-new (unknown) malware without signatures by using **AI/machine-learning file analysis** and **behavioral detection during execution**.\n\n- **AI-based Anti-Malware (pre-execution for files on disk)**\n  - NGAV uses **advanced machine learning models** that map common characteristics of malicious files.\n  - It compares a file’s **content and metadata** against these models and determines how likely the file is malicious, enabling detection of **new strains** that signature-based methods can’t catch.\n\n- **Behavioral detection (on-execution / fileless)**\n  - For **fileless malware** and other behaviors not reliant on a static file signature, the platform performs **behavioral detection and prevention while the activity is running** (e.g., attacks leveraging legitimate utilities like PowerShell/.NET).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021994: \"Windows Signature-Based Analysis FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-12-02T13:56:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000016841: \"NGAV-Based Prevention\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:11:23.000+0000)\n- Article #000019367: \"Using Artificial Intelligence\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:38:51.000+0000)\n- Article #000021990: \"What's the Difference Between an Endpoint Protection Malop and an AI Hunting Malop?\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T20:08:09.000+0000)\n- Article #000022118: \"Cybereason Coverage of Publicly Disclosed Security Vulnerabilities (CVE)\" (v2, updated 2025-06-11T22:39:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000022063: \"Malop State and Investigation Status\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:27:42.000+0000)\n- Article #000022253: \"What types of files do the NGAV and Anti-Malware > Signatures components scan?\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T19:56:57.000+0000)\n- Article #000021828: \"What Is the Difference Between \"Malware\" and a \"Malop\"?\" (v2, updated 2025-07-08T21:33:24.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0205",
      "query": "What does Sensor Grouping let me do for sensor access and policy management?",
      "ground_truth": "Sensor Grouping lets you control who can access specific sensors and helps you manage security policies more effectively.",
      "actual_answer": "Sensor Grouping lets system administrators **control which users can access which sensors** and **apply sensor security policies to sensors at scale** via groups.\n\n- **Sensor access control / delegation**\n  - Create logical sensor groups (for example by location, organizational unit, machine name, IP, OS, or FQDN) to organize sensors.\n  - Assign **Sensor Admin L1** users permissions to specific sensor groups so they can manage only those sensors.\n  - Assign **Local Analyst L1/L2** users permissions to specific sensor groups so they can **see and act only on data and MalOps related to sensors in their groups**.\n  - This helps segregate access across sub-units and reduces risk of data leakage or harmful configuration changes.\n\n- **Policy management**\n  - Apply a **sensor security policy** to a sensor group.\n  - When applied, **all existing sensors in the group and any sensors added later** adopt the group’s policy settings.\n  - **Group policy settings override** any settings previously set on an individual sensor.\n\nIf you want, tell me your Cybereason version (e.g., 24.1) and whether you’re using Local Analyst roles, and I can point to the exact UI steps under *System > Groups*.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022020: \"Sensor Grouping FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-19T13:51:12.000+0000)\n- Article #000019365: \"Task Delegation with Sensor Grouping\" (v3, updated 2026-03-06T12:38:41.000+0000)\n- Article #000015744: \"Managing Sensor Groups\" (v2, updated 2025-12-18T21:06:34.000+0000)\n- Article #000021941: \"Benefits of Sensor Grouping\" (v2, updated 2025-06-11T02:32:37.000+0000)\n- Article #000015748: \"Use Sensor Groups to Manage Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-12-18T21:07:53.000+0000)\n- Article #000016794: \"Manage Sensor Groups\" (v6, updated 2026-01-09T17:49:02.000+0000)\n- Article #000022030: \"Understanding Sensor Grouping and Transitioning\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T19:05:05.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "An Office file with VBA macros can keep generating alerts even if nobody runs it because **Cybereason Behavioral Document Protection (BDP) scans the VBA code content itself** and can detect suspicious/malicious functions **while the file is merely stored on disk**.\n\n- **BDP employs a mechanism that scans VBA code to detect functions common to malware.**\n- Because the **code content is scanned**, “**a file may trigger repeated detections just by being stored on a system, even if it is not executed**.”\n- This is more likely when the macro includes behaviors that are hard to distinguish from malware, such as:\n  - Creating/deleting/overwriting files\n  - Shell execution / executing external programs\n  - Registry operations / scheduled tasks\n  - Referencing system folders (e.g., `C:\\Windows`)\n  - Network communication\n  - Encrypted/obfuscated code\n\nSources:\n- Article #000016833: \"Fileless Protection\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T21:09:11.000+0000)\n- Article #000023704: \"False Positives for VBA Macros\" (v3, updated 2026-02-03T12:15:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000021914: \"Security Value of Behavioral Document Protection\" (v2, updated 2025-06-18T21:46:09.000+0000)\n- Article #000022382: \"Threat Alert: Microsoft Office Exploit (CVE-2021-40444)\" (v2, updated 2026-01-30T17:17:04.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "For Windows 8 and earlier endpoints, you must **manually install the DigiCert Global Root G2 root CA certificate** into the **Local Machine** certificate store (machine keystore) to avoid interrupted connections when Cybereason updates to the G2 certificate chain starting February 2026.\n\n**What to do (manual install on Win8 and earlier):**\n1.       "query": "Why would sensors CSV not match Sensors page when env is busy and list huge?",
      "ground_truth": "In very active environments with large outputs (over 50k sensors), the download call can be delayed (1–2 minutes) and the UI can lag even longer. Sensors updated/installed during list generation can cause mismatches between the CSV and the UI list.",
      "actual_answer": "When the environment is very active and the sensors list is very large (for example, >50,000 sensors), the CSV export and the Sensors page can show different data because the two views are not generated at the exact same moment and both can lag during heavy/large requests.\n\nKey reasons noted in the KB:\n\n- **Export “weight” and processing delay:** Generating a CSV with **50–60k sensors can take 1–2 minutes** (depending on the environment). During that time, sensors may be **installed/updated/changed**, so the exported snapshot can differ from what the UI shows.  \n- **UI update delay:** The **UI server can take longer to get updates**, so the Sensors page may reflect changes later (or differently) than the CSV generation timing.\n- **High-change environments amplify timing gaps:** If sensors are being **updated/installed during the period you generate/download the list**, this can directly impact mismatches.\n\nHow to investigate (per the KB):\n\n1. **Compare the two lists** (e.g., in Excel) to identify specific sensors that differ.  \n2. For those sensors, **check whether they were updated/installed during the export/UI refresh window**, as that timing can explain the mismatch.\n\nIf you’re exporting via API, note that (in some versions) exporting **more than 10,000 sensors** could also result in an **incomplete** CSV export; this was described as resolved in release notes.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021321: \"Investigate Mismatches in Sensors CSV and Sensor List\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T19:49:36.000+0000)\n- Article #000023124: \"23.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-18T19:49:35.000+0000)\n- Article #000023127: \"22.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-14T18:42:18.000+0000)\n- Article #000016779: \"Sensor Tagging\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T20:37:45.000+0000)\n- Article #000023132: \"24.1 All Versions\" (v14, updated 2026-03-12T16:58:35.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "To determine whether the Cybereason sensor is blocking printing due to **malicious-behavior prevention** or an **application conflict**, use the following checks from the Knowledge Base:\n\n- **Run the “alert test” (primary indicator)**\n  - Ask the user to **uninstall/remove the sensor** and confirm whether the printer works normally afterward.\n  - If printing works without the sensor, it supports that the sensor is involved (either via detection/prevention or via conflict).\n\n- **If you suspect an application conflict, collect the right logs**\n  -       "query": "To move a sensor to another detection server, what config key/value do I change?",
      "ground_truth": "Update the detection server FQDN in the sensor config by changing the server.host value (MacOS uses host instead).",
      "actual_answer": "Change the **Detection Server hostname (FQDN)** saved in the sensor configuration:\n\n- **Windows:** edit the Registry at `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SOFTWARE\\Cybereason\\ActiveProbe` and change the **`server.host`** value to the target Detection Server **FQDN**.\n- **macOS:** edit `/usr/local/cybereason/config.plist` and change the **`host`** value (note: macOS uses `host`, not `server.host`) to the target Detection Server **FQDN**.\n- **Linux:** edit `/opt/cybereason/sensor/etc/sensor.conf` and change the **`server.host`** value to the target Detection Server **FQDN**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021309: \"How to Manually Move a Single Sensor between Detection Servers\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T19:31:09.000+0000)\n- Article #000016246: \"Update Sensors\" (v3, updated 2026-01-12T21:29:40.000+0000)\n- Article #000016782: \"Upgrade Sensors\" (v7, updated 2026-02-26T15:31:51.000+0000)\n- Article #000021346: \"Best Practices for Using Proxies with the Sensor\" (v2, updated 2025-07-10T19:10:52.000+0000)\n- Article #000021911: \"Registration Server FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-18T19:48:24.000+0000)\n- Article #000016908: \"Manage Sites\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:35:28.000+0000)",

      "ground_truth": "Check the Catalina logs on the perspective; the username is recorded there even when the user-audit log shows it empty.",
      "actual_answer": "The blank username in **User Audit Log login events** can often be recovered by checking the **Catalina logs on the WebApp server (Perspective)** that generated the log entry.\n\n- Cybereason builds the audit logs by extracting fields from the request; in some cases (especially **certificate/auto-process logins**) the username field isn’t extracted, so `cs1=/` appears in the audit syslog entry.\n- To find the actual user:\n  - Identify the **machineIP / machineName** in the User Audit log entry (e.g., `cs5Label=machineIP cs5=10.16.0.108`).\n  - On the corresponding server (the WebApp/Perspective server for that IP), check the **Catalina logs** for the matching timestamp; the Catalina logs may include lines like:  \n    `User <username> logged in using a Client SSL Cert...`\n- If the activity is from an automated process (often a **Jenkins job**), the Catalina logs plus the source IP can help identify it (example found in the KB: `jenkins_api@cybereason.com`).\n- If this happens frequently, the KB notes you may need to **log in to the server (based on the IP) and locate the job causing it**, typically with **DevOps assistance**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021312: \"Empty Username in User Audit Log\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T19:37:41.000+0000)\n- Article #000020858: \"How to Retrieve User Audit Logs\" (v2, updated 2025-06-10T13:35:30.000+0000)\n- Article #000015326: \"Audit Log\" (v7, updated 2026-03-09T17:24:07.000+0000)",

      "query": "Why would a sensor upgrade delete a DLL and then the service won't start?",
      "ground_truth": "During some upgrades, Windows MSI can unexpectedly remove the existing DLL when its version is higher than the DLL in the new package, and then not install a replacement. This results in the service failing with a \"DLL was not found\" error.",

      "ground_truth": "The UI can’t retrieve IP reputation unless the IP is included in the client’s custom reputation list. Otherwise, the client must upload it or use the API to access tokens table data.",
      "actual_answer": "IP reputation lookup shows **“No reputation found”** because **the Cybereason UI (Security Profile > Reputations) does not support looking up arbitrary IP reputations**—this is a **product limitation**.\n\n- In the **Reputation Search UI**, IP reputation results are available **only for IPs included in your custom reputation file/list**. If the IP isn’t in that custom list, the UI returns **“No reputation found.”**\n- Cybereason reputation lookups involve **Sage Private** (on the customer server) and **Sage Global**. **IP reputations exist in Sage Global’s “tokens” table**, and **the UI doesn’t retrieve IP reputation from there** (unless it’s in the custom list).\n\nWhat you can do instead:\n- **Add/upload the IP to your custom reputation list** (so it can be found in the UI).\n- Use the **IP Reputation API** (`/rest/download_v1/ip_reputation`) to retrieve IP reputations programmatically.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021853: \"\"No Reputation Found\" Error When Searching for IP Reputation in the Security Profile Screen\" (v4, updated 2025-12-01T22:00:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000021290: \"Address an Error for IP Reputations - No reputation found\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T22:15:57.000+0000)\n- Article #000016943: \"Manage Reputations\" (v6, updated 2025-11-24T21:49:36.000+0000)\n- Article #000022913: \"Retrieve IP Address Reputations\" (v3, updated 2025-10-31T19:32:49.000+0000)",
      "correctness": 4,

      "reasoning": "Matches the reference’s core point: the UI only returns IP reputation if the IP is in the client’s custom reputation list; otherwise you must upload it or use an API.       "query": "When should we run re-export script for missing elements—graph vs Elasticsearch mismatch?",
      "ground_truth": "Consider a re-export when elements exist in the Graph but are missing from Elasticsearch. Confirm by querying both Graph and Elasticsearch.",
      "actual_answer": "Run a re-export **only when you’ve confirmed the missing element exists in the Transparency Graph but is not present in Elasticsearch (ES)**.\n\n- In DI environments, the data flow is: **Sensor → Transparency (Graph) → Kafka (queue) → Elasticsearch**\n- The UI queries data from **Elasticsearch**, so “missing elements” in the UI can occur when:\n  - The element **is in the Graph**, but\n  - The element **didn’t get exported/indexed into ES**\n- In that specific **Graph vs ES mismatch** scenario, re-export is relevant—**verify by querying both Graph and ES first**.\n\nImportant notes from the KB:\n- **Use of the re-export script must be approved by the R&D team and tracked in a Jira.**\n- The KB notes that using the script **limits your ability to find the root cause** of why the data went missing, so it should not be the first step until the mismatch is confirmed.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021272: \"When to Consider a Re-Export of Elements\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T21:31:17.000+0000)\n- Article #000021095: \"Re-Export Elements by Type to DI from VC Transparency\" (v2, updated 2026-01-06T21:08:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000022499: \"How to Re-Export Elements to DI\" (v3, updated 2025-12-22T14:47:36.000+0000)\n- Article #000021730: \"Troubleshooting Missing Data for MalOps\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:46:25.000+0000)",

      "query": "InnoDB file-in-use error on client MySQL—what should we try first to confirm CR is causing it?",
      "ground_truth": "Have the client disable Cybereason on one test device and check whether the error still reproduces to confirm if the sensor is the cause.",
      "actual_answer": "To first confirm whether Cybereason is causing the InnoDB “file-in-use” error, **disable Cybereason on one test device and check if the issue is still reproducible**.\n\nThen, if you need more confirmation:\n\n- **Check timing vs. AV scans:** The sensor may temporarily lock files during an AV scan, so compare the error timestamp to scan activity.\n- **Identify the locking process:** Use **Microsoft Process Monitor** to determine which process is touching/locking the MySQL/InnoDB database files and triggering the error.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021267: \"MySQL Common Errors for the Cybereason Platform\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T21:18:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000021694: \"\"The File You Uploaded is Invalid\" Error Displays While Importing CSV File\" (v4, updated 2025-12-01T22:04:06.000+0000)\n- Article #000021597: \"Errors When Trying to Upload Custom Reputation List\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:19:37.000+0000)\n- Article #000021489: \"Troubleshooting Custom Reputation List Uploads\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:46:00.000+0000)\n- Article #000021626: \"Troubleshooting Server Stability Issues\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:50:57.000+0000)",

      "ground_truth": "Reinstall the sensor, then edit /opt/cybereason/sensor/etc/sensor.conf to remove server.host=127.0.0.1 and set server.signon_host to the registration IP (plus signon_port and organization). Restart the cybereason-sensor service.",
      "actual_answer": "Edit the Linux sensor configuration so it uses the Registration server (signon) host/port instead of `127.0.0.1`.\n\n- On the endpoint, go to:\n  - `/opt/cybereason/sensor/etc`\n- Edit `sensor.conf`:\n  - Remove: `server.host=127.0.0.1`\n  - Add (with your environment/account values):\n    - `server.signon_host={registration IP}`\n    - `server.signon_port={port - usually 443/8443}`\n    - `server.organization={account name}`\n- Restart the sensor:\n  - `sudo systemctl stop cybereason-sensor`\n  - `sudo systemctl start cybereason-sensor`\n\nWhat the KB also notes (root cause): this can happen if the installer couldn’t populate the registration address due to an unsupported/missing Python setup.       "query_id": "tc_0439",
      "query": "How do I archive a sensor directly in Postgres when API fails?",
      "ground_truth": "Update the sensor record in the sm.sensors table by setting status to 'Archive' for the target machine_name. The UI should reflect the change within a few minutes.",
      "actual_answer": "To archive a sensor directly in Postgres when the API fails, you can update the sensor’s status in the `sm.sensors` table (this is considered a “bad practice” and should be used only when the API isn’t an option or sensor records are corrupted).\n\n**Procedure (DB method):**\n1. **Log in to the Postgres database** (customer Scribe/Postgres DB access is typically support-only).\n2. **Find the sensor record and check its current status**:\n   ```sql\n   select * from sm.sensors where machine_name = 'xxxxxxx';\n   ```\n3. **If the current status is not `Archive`, update it to `Archive`:**\n   ```sql\n   update sm.sensors set status='Archive' where machine_name = 'xxxxxxx';\n   ```\n4. **Confirm the change** by re-running the select query:\n   ```sql\n   select * from sm.sensors where machine_name = 'xxxxxxx';\n   ```\n5. **Wait a few minutes** for the UI to reflect the updated status.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021262: \"Move Sensors to Archive Manually\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T21:10:55.000+0000)\n- Article #000022961: \"Archive Sensor\" (v4, updated 2025-10-31T15:12:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000015736: \"Stale and Archived Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-12-18T21:02:07.000+0000)\n- Article #000021277: \"Investigate a Failed Export of the Sensor List\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T21:37:46.000+0000)\n- Article #000022967: \"Restore a Removed Sensor\" (v3, updated 2025-10-31T19:24:30.000+0000)",

      "ground_truth": "Closing a Restricted Remote Shell session runs a command that disables PSRemoting. This behavior happens only in restricted mode, not unrestricted.",
      "actual_answer": "WinRM/PSRemoting stops working after you exit **Restricted Remote Shell** because the Restricted Remote Shell feature **explicitly disables PSRemoting when the session closes**.\n\nFrom the Knowledge Base:\n\n- When Restricted Remote Shell opens a session, it runs:\n  - `powershell.exe -c \"Enable-PSRemoting -SkipNetworkProfileCheck -Force; Register-PSSessionConfiguration -Name CybereasonConfig -Path C:\\ProgramData\\apv2\\Output\\Restrictions.pssc -Force\"`\n- When the Restricted Remote Shell session is closed, it runs:\n  - `powershell.exe -c \"Unregister-PSSessionConfiguration -Name CybereasonConfig -Force; Disable-PSRemoting -Force\"`\n\nAs a result:\n- PSRemoting (and therefore WinRM-based remote access) can stop working for customers who rely on it after they close a **restricted** remote shell session.\n- The KB notes this **only happens in Restricted Remote Shell** and **does not occur in Unrestricted mode**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021255: \"Restricted Remote Shell disables PSRemoting\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T20:59:43.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0447",
      "query": "Remote Shell dies after 5 mins idle—what causes it and how to recover?",
      "ground_truth": "It happens due to at least five minutes of inactivity between the server and Remote Shell. Click Reconnect to start the session again.",
      "actual_answer": "Remote Shell sessions end after 5 minutes of inactivity because Cybereason enforces a **default 5‑minute inactivity timeout**; when there’s no interaction between the Cybereason server and the Remote Shell utility for at least five minutes, the UI closes the session.\n\n**Cause**\n- **No activity for 5 minutes:** “There was no interaction between your Cybereason server and the Remote Shell utility for at least five minutes,” so the server ends the Remote Shell session.\n- **Lengthy operations can also trigger the same 5‑minute timeout:** Remote Shell may time out during long-running actions (for example, downloading/copying a large file), closing the session and killing the process.\n\n**How to recover**\n- In the Remote Shell window, click **Reconnect** to reestablish the connection/session.\n- If the session ended due to a **network disconnection**, it may take **up to 5 minutes** before you can reestablish a new session to that machine (and reconnection must be initiated manually—Cybereason does not auto-reconnect).\n\n**If you need more than 5 minutes**\n- The default timeout is **5 minutes**. To change it, **contact Cybereason Technical Support** (note: timeout changes are **not retained** after platform upgrades or certain restarts; you’ll need to re-request the change via your CSM/Support after those events).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021806: \"What Errors might I Encounter When Using Remote Shell?\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T20:01:54.000+0000)\n- Article #000016814: \"Respond to Threats on a Machine with Remote Shell\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T21:01:05.000+0000)\n- Article #000021958: \"Remote Shell Usage Errors\" (v2, updated 2025-06-18T20:21:06.000+0000)\n- Article #000021992: \"Remote Shell Times Out While Running Lengthy Operations\" (v2, updated 2025-06-18T20:19:05.000+0000)",

      "query": "If curl PUT fails, how do I set Sage proxy URL on the on-prem perspective server?",
      "ground_truth": "Update the SAGE_GLOBAL configuration in MongoDB to set proxyUrl to https://<proxy_address>:<port_number>. Then restart the tomcat service.",
      "actual_answer": "If the `curl PUT` to the local configuration service fails and the changes aren’t applied, set the Sage proxy URL directly in MongoDB on the on‑prem Perspective server, then restart Tomcat.\n\n- **Confirm the PUT isn’t applying changes**\n  - `curl --tlsv1.2 -kLs -X PUT https://localhost:$((\\`facter configured_probe_port\\`+10000))/rest/configuration/configurationServer/edit --header 'content-type: application/json' -d @config.txt`\n  - Verify it didn’t change:\n    - `curl --tlsv1.2 -kLs -X GET https://localhost:$((\\`facter configured_probe_port\\`+10000))/rest/configuration/configurationServers >> config.txt`\n\n- **Take a Mongo backup**\n  - `mongodump -o /tmp/mongo<date>`\n\n- **Set the proxy URL in MongoDB**\n  - `mongo cybereason`\n  - Run:\n    - `db.cp_server_configuration.update({\"cpType\" : \"SAGE_GLOBAL\"}, {$set: {\"proxyUrl\" : \"https://<proxy_address>:<port_number>\"}})`\n  - Note: The proxy address must be **http or https**.\n\n- **Verify the change**\n  - `db.cp_server_configuration.find()`\n  - Confirm the `SAGE_GLOBAL` entry shows `proxyUrl : \"https://<proxy_address>:<port_number>\"`\n\n- **Restart Tomcat** on the Perspective server to apply the change.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000020988: \"Workaround: How to Configure Access to sage.cybereason.com via Proxy in Case CURL Does Not Work\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T19:50:58.000+0000)\n- Article #000021595: \"Error: Cannot Get BWL/Custom Detection Rules\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:18:57.000+0000)\n- Article #000020932: \"Configure Private Sage Proxy using the API\" (v3, updated 2025-11-25T21:46:04.000+0000)\n- Article #000021315: \"\"Proxy for reputation check\" Troubleshooting in On-Prem Environments\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T19:41:22.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0486",
      "query": "On-prem detection server: how do I manually unblock sensors when UI/script fails?",
      "ground_truth": "SSH to the Detection server, back up /etc/sysconfig/iptables, remove the two top DROP rules, then restart iptables. Verify with iptables -L that the DROP rules are gone.",
      "actual_answer": "To manually unblock sensors on an **on-prem Detection server** when unblocking from the **Management UI** fails (and the standard script doesn’t work), remove the firewall “DROP” rules from the Detection server’s iptables configuration and restart iptables.\n\nSteps (on the affected Detection server)\n1. **SSH** to the Detection server.\n2. **Back up** the iptables config file:\n   - `cp /etc/sysconfig/iptables /etc/sysconfig/iptables.bck`\n3. **Edit** `/etc/sysconfig/iptables` and **delete the two “DROP” rules at the top** of the file.\n4. **Save** the file and **restart** iptables:\n   - `service iptables restart`\n5. **Verify** the active firewall rules no longer include those DROP rules:\n   - `iptables -L`\n\nResult\n- Sensors will be **unblocked on that specific Detection server**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000020875: \"How to Unblock Sensors Manually for On-Prem Environments\" (v2, updated 2026-01-06T20:47:29.000+0000)\n- Article #000021927: \"Supported Capabilities for Offline Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T21:03:26.000+0000)\n- Article #000022304: \"Troubleshooting Sensor Log Error Messages\" (v5, updated 2025-12-03T22:00:41.000+0000)\n- Article #000021505: \"Sensor Connectivity Issues - Troubleshooting\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:03:17.000+0000)\n- Article #000021772: \"Sensor UI Shows All Sensors as Offline\" (v2, updated 2025-09-05T20:25:36.000+0000)\n- Article #000023124: \"23.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-18T19:49:35.000+0000)\n- Article #000021240: \"How to Troubleshoot On-Premise Detection Server High CPU Usage\" (v2, updated 2025-12-29T18:11:40.000+0000)\n- Article #000023094: \"23.2 All Versions\" (v18, updated 2026-01-27T14:08:31.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "Open the customer’s network access to the Yum repositories—this issue is caused by the server timing out while trying to reach the configured Yum repo URLs during the on-prem installation.\n\n**How to recognize the issue**\n- You see many **Timeout** errors from Yum repositories.\n- Running `puppet agent -t` takes **15–20 minutes** and then fails with timeout errors.\n\n**Fix**\n- Have the customer **open/allow the required network connectivity** (firewall/proxy/routing/DNS as applicable) from the server to the Yum repositories.\n\n**How to verify it’s fixed**\n- Run:\n  - `yum update`  \n    - You should see packages updating and the server reaching the Yum repositories.\n  - `curl -s --dump-header - yum repolist rhcd -v | grep Repo-baseurl | awk '{print $2}' -o /dev/null`  \n    - You should receive **HTTP 200 OK**.\n  - `yum repolist rhcd -v`  \n    - Repos should list successfully (no timeouts).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000020946: \"No Connection to Yum Repositories Issue\" (v2, updated 2026-01-06T20:25:56.000+0000)\n- Article #000020863: \"How to Check and Install Missing Packages for Linux Sensor Installations\" (v4, updated 2025-12-01T21:13:57.000+0000)\n- Article #000016904: \"Pre-installation Requirements and Instructions\" (v9, updated 2026-03-17T01:33:50.000+0000)\n- Article #000020855: \"Install Linux dependencies for the Cybereason Sensor\" (v2, updated 2025-12-30T14:11:50.000+0000)\n- Article #000022755: \"eBPF Linux Framework - Feature Handoff\" (v2, updated 2025-12-04T22:25:28.000+0000)\n- Article #000021767: \"TFA Users Unable to Connect (On-Prem)\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:42:03.000+0000)",

      "query": "How do I quickly filter KnownMalware alerts to just the last 24 hours?",
      "ground_truth": "Use the malware feed URL with a timestamp filter set to 86400000 and type set to KnownMalware. The document provides the exact link to apply this last-24-hours filter.",
      "actual_answer": "To filter **KnownMalware** alerts to **only the last 24 hours**, query the **malware** collection in MongoDB using the alert `type` and a `timestamp` range (timestamps are **Unix time in milliseconds**).\n\n- Convert “now” and “now minus 24 hours” to **Unix epoch (milliseconds)**.\n- Run a count first to validate the filter:\n\n```js\ndb.malware.find({\n  type: 'KnownMalware',\n  timestamp: { $gte: <START_EPOCH_MS>, $lt: <END_EPOCH_MS> }\n}).count()\n```\n\nWhere:\n- `<END_EPOCH_MS>` = current time in epoch milliseconds\n- `<START_EPOCH_MS>` = `<END_EPOCH_MS> - 24 hours` (in ms)\n\nThe Knowledge Base examples confirm:\n- `type:'KnownMalware'` can be used to target known malware alerts.\n- `timestamp` filtering is done with Unix time **in milliseconds** using `$gte` / `$lt`.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000023113: \"21.2 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-13T19:59:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000021118: \"How to Delete all Malware Alerts\" (v3, updated 2025-12-01T21:23:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000016860: \"Set the Anti-Malware Modes\" (v5, updated 2025-11-24T21:17:34.000+0000)\n- Article #000023683: \"Delete Malware Alerts in Bulk\" (v1, updated 2025-11-14T16:29:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000022479: \"How to Handle False Positive Detections\" (v3, updated 2025-10-02T14:53:47.000+0000)\n- Article #000022463: \"XDR - Using PubSub to Consume Received Alerts\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T21:24:25.000+0000)\n- Article #000022978: \"Create a Sensor Policy\" (v4, updated 2025-10-31T15:22:09.000+0000)\n- Article #000022794: \"Reduce Recurring File Events by the Same Process and Event Type - Feature Handoff\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:19:31.000+0000)",

      "query": "Fix for corrupted local blocklist DB causing allowlisted apps to get blocked?",
      "ground_truth": "Disable App Control, delete C:\\ProgramData\\crb1\\_blockListFile.db, then re-enable App Control and wait for the DB file to be recreated.",
      "actual_answer": "Use the workaround to refresh the sensor’s local Blocklist DB by deleting the corrupted/outdated local DB file and letting the sensor re-download it.\n\nSteps (workaround):\n- On the affected machine, reproduce the issue by running the application to confirm it is being prevented.\n- Disable **App Control** on that machine (verify in the UI that App Control is disabled).\n- Delete the local DB file on the endpoint:\n  - `C:\\ProgramData\\crb1\\_blockListFile.db`\n- Re-enable **App Control** on the sensor and wait for `_blockListFile.db` to be recreated.\n- Run the previously blocked application again and confirm it is no longer prevented.\n\nResult:\n- The endpoint downloads a fresh Blocklist DB (aligned with other sensors in the environment), and legitimate allowlisted apps should stop being blocked.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000020961: \"Local BlocklistDB is Not Up to Date or Corrupted\" (v2, updated 2025-12-31T12:35:10.000+0000)\n- Article #000021528: \"Application Control Repeatedly Prevents an Application from Running\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T18:21:21.000+0000)\n- Article #000021557: \"File on the Blocklist Still Running\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T19:26:06.000+0000)\n- Article #000022295: \"Troubleshooting and Fixing Application Blocking on Mobile Devices\" (v5, updated 2025-12-03T21:43:42.000+0000)\n- Article #000016391: \"Allowlists and Blocklists\" (v2, updated 2026-01-13T18:45:06.000+0000)\n- Article #000021613: \"MalOp Allowlist Does Not Work Due to Connection Issue\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:52:05.000+0000)",

      "query": "If suspect processes show up in malop but not ES, what’s next check?",
      "ground_truth": "Next, check whether the suspectsProcesses exist in the feature analyzer (graph) by searching based on the MalOp.",
      "actual_answer": "Next, check whether the MalOp is being driven by something **other than a “normal” process record in ES**—most commonly a **floating module** detection.\n\n- **Check the MalOp’s Suspicions text**\n  - If you see something like **“Detected by PowerShell & .NET protection (ATT&CK: Execution – PowerShell)”** but you can’t find an actual PowerShell process, this can be **by design**: the MalOp may be tied to a **floating module** (for example, a **.NET module floating in memory** inside an EXE), not a PowerShell process.\n- **Check for floating-module related MalOps/detections**\n  - “Suspicious Execution of PowerShell” can be caused by **.NET floating modules** (introduced in **19.0**) and therefore may not map cleanly to a PowerShell process you expect to see.\n- **If you need to reduce/adjust this behavior**\n  - In the relevant **sensor policy**, go to **Fileless Protection** and adjust the sensitivity for **“.NET floating modules”**.\n\nWhat I *didn’t* find in the provided KB context: a specific ES troubleshooting checklist for why a MalOp “suspect process” wouldn’t appear in ES (e.g., data retention, query scope, collection gaps).       "actual_answer": "No. **By design, ActiveConsole cannot be newer than Minionhost on a sensor.**\n\n- Cybereason notes that **Minionhost (ActiveProbe) and ActiveConsole are different components**, and during **minor upgrades** only Minionhost may upgrade.\n- Therefore it’s possible to see **Minionhost version > ActiveConsole version**.\n- The reverse (**Minionhost version < ActiveConsole version**, meaning ActiveConsole newer than Minionhost) **“is not possible, by design.”**\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022367: \"How to View Sensor Versions\" (v3, updated 2025-12-30T13:03:13.000+0000)\n- Article #000022319: \"Sensor Platform - Overview for Support\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T19:07:10.000+0000)\n- Article #000021600: \"Sensors Do Not Publish Data after Upgrade\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:24:42.000+0000)\n- Article #000023124: \"23.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-18T19:49:35.000+0000)\n- Article #000022395: \"New Sensor vs. Old Sensor for Mac Endpoints\" (v2, updated 2025-06-17T18:31:37.000+0000)\n- Article #000023127: \"22.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-14T18:42:18.000+0000)",

      "query": "How do I confirm Transparency is actually consuming SOC federation mapping msgs?",
      "ground_truth": "Check the Transparency’s Pub/Sub subscription and review the Oldest unacked message metric; rising values indicate messages aren’t being consumed.",
      "actual_answer": "To confirm a Transparency is consuming SOC Federation mapping messages, verify it at both the Pub/Sub subscription level and on the Transparency host:\n\n- **Check the Transparency’s Pub/Sub subscription metrics (GCP Console)**\n  - Open the **subscription** that belongs to the specific Transparency.\n  - Review the **Oldest unacked message** metric:\n    - If **Oldest unacked message increases**, messages are **not being consumed** as expected.\n    - If there are only **brief spikes**, or **no oldest unacked message shown**, messages are being consumed (or no messages are arriving—verify publishing separately).\n\n- **Validate consumption in the Transparency log**\n  - SSH to the Transparency server.\n  - Check: `/opt/cybereason/logs/socFederation.log`\n  - This log “lists all the messages consumed by the Transparency” and should show entries like:\n    - `Got federation mapping update SensorGroupMappingMessage ...`\n  - If you requested a re-sync, confirm the consumed update is marked with `isSync=true` in the same log.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021189: \"How to Verify that SOC Federation was Properly Configured\" (v2, updated 2025-12-29T22:30:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000022684: \"SOC Federation - Handoff\" (v1, updated 2025-06-10T14:19:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000022527: \"How to Investigate a Wrong SOC Federation Mapping\" (v3, updated 2025-12-08T20:46:32.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0544",
      "query": "High CPU on on-prem detection: what top output indicates Java full GC vs general load?",
      "ground_truth": "If one CPU core is pegged at 100% while the others are near 0%, it indicates a Java Full GC issue. If all cores are around 90–100%, it’s general high CPU utilization.",
      "actual_answer": "On an on-prem Detection Server, the `top` CPU pattern distinguishes **general high load** from **Java Full GC** as follows:\n\n- **General high CPU / general load**\n  - In `top`, press **`1`** to show per-core usage.\n  - **Indicator:** **All (or most) CPU cores are high (around 90–100%)**.\n  - Meaning (per KB): general high CPU that loads the server, but it doesn’t “stick” on one core.\n\n- **Java Full GC**\n  - In `top` with per-core view enabled (press **`1`**):\n  - **Indicator:** **One CPU core is at ~100% while the other cores are near 0%**.\n  - Meaning (per KB): the server is busy cleaning Java memory (Full GC), sensors may disconnect, and the Detection Servers page may show no connected-sensor info.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021240: \"How to Troubleshoot On-Premise Detection Server High CPU Usage\" (v2, updated 2025-12-29T18:11:40.000+0000)\n- Article #000021500: \"Warning - Showing Data from Only Some Machines\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T22:05:27.000+0000)\n- Article #000020989: \"Environment Analysis Due to Performance Issue\" (v3, updated 2025-12-01T20:59:30.000+0000)\n- Article #000022312: \"Tier 4 - Common and Important Cases\" (v2, updated 2025-06-23T14:29:44.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "To fix an uninstall failure caused by the **Protected Service not being removed**, make these registry edits (then reboot) before retrying the uninstall:\n\n- **Prerequisite:** Ensure **Sensor Tampering protection is disabled** (if it’s enabled, you won’t be able to proceed with uninstallation).\n\n1) Open **Registry Editor** and set:\n   - `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SOFTWARE\\Cybereason\\ActiveProbe`\n     - Change the value **`installElam`** to **`0`**\n\n2) In the Protected Service key, delete a specific value:\n   - `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\CybereasonProtectedSvc`\n     - Delete the value **`LaunchProtected`**\n\n3) **Reboot** the machine.\n\n4) **Retry the sensor uninstall**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021103: \"How to Uninstall a Sensor Due to a Protected Service Failure\" (v2, updated 2025-12-29T18:14:45.000+0000)\n- Article #000021795: \"Sensor Uninstall Fails with an Error\" (v3, updated 2025-09-05T20:27:28.000+0000)\n- Article #000021552: \"Uninstall Failed to Remove Cybereason Driver (CrDrv)\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:54:49.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "Drop the recording zip files on the Detection server under **`/opt/cybereason/to_play/all/<date>/`** (where `<date>` is today’s date), then run the playback script.\n\nProcedure (on-prem Detection server):\n1. (Recommended) Block sensor connections:\n   - `/opt/puppet-cybereason/manage/upgrade/1block_aps.sh`\n2. Create the destination folder:\n   - `mkdir -p /opt/cybereason/to_play/all/<date>`\n3. Ensure **all recording zip files are in the same directory** (not nested in per-day subfolders). If needed, copy them up into the main folder.\n5. Set ownership to tomcat:\n   - `chown tomcat:tomcat /opt/cybereason/to_play/all/<date>/*`\n6.       "ground_truth": "Upgrade actions for offline sensors stay in pending status for up to three days. If the sensor is still offline after that, the action times out and must be re-run.",
      "actual_answer": "A queued sensor upgrade for an offline endpoint stays **Pending for up to 3 days** by default.\n\n- If the sensor comes online within those **3 days**, the upgrade runs automatically.\n- If the sensor is still offline after **3 days**, the action **times out** (appears as **“Timed Out”**) and you must **re-run** the upgrade action.\n- The **3-day queue period can be customized**—you’ll need to **contact Cybereason Technical Support** to change it.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021921: \"Gradual Sensor Upgrade FAQ\" (v3, updated 2025-12-29T13:58:16.000+0000)\n- Article #000022066: \"Scaled Sensor Upgrade Process - FAQ\" (v2, updated 2025-06-18T21:08:10.000+0000)\n- Article #000023130: \"21.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-13T16:51:08.000+0000)\n- Article #000016793: \"Monitor and Manage Sensors\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T20:50:14.000+0000)\n- Article #000021927: \"Supported Capabilities for Offline Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T21:03:26.000+0000)\n- Article #000021371: \"Gradual and Automatic Sensor Upgrades - Handoff\" (v3, updated 2025-12-05T21:04:00.000+0000)",

      "ground_truth": "Update the Local update server URL in the sensor policy Anti-Malware screen and click Save & Publish. Then go to System > Sensors, select the sensors, and run Actions > Update to apply the new configuration.",

      "query_id": "tc_0611",
      "query": "How do I validate Cybereason Anti-Malware is working on an endpoint?",
      "ground_truth": "Run the EICAR antivirus test file on a machine with Anti-Malware enabled. It should be detected or removed based on the sensor policy configuration.",
      "actual_answer": "To validate Cybereason **Anti-Malware** is working on an endpoint, run the **EICAR antivirus test file** on a machine where Anti-Malware is enabled and confirm it is detected/removed per your policy.\n\n### Validate Anti-Malware (Signatures) using EICAR\n1. Ensure the endpoint is in a sensor policy with **Anti-Malware enabled** (Cybereason recommends testing on a **single sensor** in its own policy to avoid excessive alerts).\n2. Download the **EICAR Standard Anti-Virus Test** file.\n3. Execute the EICAR test file on the endpoint.\n4. Confirm the file is **detected or removed** according to the endpoint’s Anti-Malware policy configuration.  \n   *Note: EICAR is safe but designed to trigger AV detection.*\n\n### Optional checks (endpoint-side status visibility)\n- On the endpoint, right-click the Cybereason system tray icon to view **Anti-Malware > Signatures mode** details such as:\n  - whether Signatures mode is installing / scan status\n  - last signature update time\n  - last full/quick scan time\n  - signature DB version\n\n### If detection doesn’t occur\n- The Knowledge Base notes Anti-Malware Signatures mode is intended to run **without third-party antivirus tools in parallel**; presence of another AV can render Signatures mode **not fully functional**. If needed, check for remaining third-party AV components (services/processes/apps).\n\nSources:\n- Article #000020841: \"How to Verify the Proper Function of Endpoint Features\" (v2, updated 2025-12-11T16:14:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000011323: \"Configure Anti-Malware\" (v3, updated 2025-11-20T18:03:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000016282: \"Endpoint Prevention\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T21:58:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000016860: \"Set the Anti-Malware Modes\" (v5, updated 2025-11-24T21:17:34.000+0000)\n- Article #000022479: \"How to Handle False Positive Detections\" (v3, updated 2025-10-02T14:53:47.000+0000)\n- Article #000016769: \"Endpoint Machine Notifications and Desktop Settings\" (v3, updated 2025-11-24T20:33:50.000+0000)\n- Article #000021478: \"Signature Protection Related information Not Displayed for Right Clicking on Cybereason Icon in System Tray\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:31:40.000+0000)",

      "query": "AmSvc log shows huge KB for sig DB updates—what do those numbers actually mean?",
      "ground_truth": "Those KB values in the AmSvc logs are not the actual transferred download size. They represent all patches and don’t account for compression.",
      "actual_answer": "Those “KB” values in **AmSvc.log** are **not the actual amount of data transferred over the network** for the Signature DB update. They represent the **total size of all patches** included in the update calculation and **do not account for compression**, so summing them will greatly overstate real network usage.\n\nFrom the Knowledge Base:\n- Log lines like `updater.cpp:362 The update for the database will download 20771 KB` reflect **all patches** and **ignore compression**.\n- To see the **real network traffic** for AmSvc, measure it via the Cybereason UI:\n  - Go to **Investigation**\n  - Build a query with:\n    - **Connection** (no filter)\n    - **Owner process** filter: *Process name matches pattern* `*amsvc*`\n    - **Owner machine** filter: *Machine name matches word* `{your machine name}`\n  - Return to **Connection** and **Get results**\n  - Review the **Received bytes** column to see actual transferred data.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000022462: \"How to Measure the Signature DB Download\" (v3, updated 2025-12-08T22:46:50.000+0000)\n- Article #000022008: \"How to Verify the Signatures Database Version\" (v2, updated 2025-06-17T12:31:45.000+0000)\n- Article #000022197: \"AMSVC.exe Process Uses Larger Amounts of Commit Memory than Expected - Workaround\" (v2, updated 2025-06-10T22:41:59.000+0000)\n- Article #000021293: \"Investigate BDP Performance Issues\" (v2, updated 2026-01-08T22:29:21.000+0000)",

      "query": "How do I bulk clear all malware alerts stuck in Need your Attention?",
      "ground_truth": "SSH to the UI server, back up MongoDB, then run a Mongo update on the cybereason DB to set needsAttention from true to false for all records.",
      "actual_answer": "To bulk clear **all Malware alerts** (including those in **“Needs your attention”**) you must delete them directly from the **MongoDB `malware` collection** on the UI/Perspective server.\n\n**Warning:** This process involves editing MongoDB—**take a backup first**.\n\n## Procedure (delete ALL malware alerts)\n1. **SSH to the customer UI (Perspective/Webapp) server**\n2. Become root:\n   - `sudo su`\n3. **Create a backup directory**:\n   - `mkdir /tmp/mongodump-$(date +\"%d-%m-%Y\")`\n4. **Back up MongoDB**:\n   - `mongodump -o /tmp/mongodump-<date-folder-created-above>`\n5. **Open MongoDB shell**:\n   - `mongo cybereason`\n6. **(Optional) Count current malware alerts**:\n   - `db.malware.find().count()`\n7. **Delete ALL malware alerts** (can take time; example notes 3–5 minutes for ~3 million alerts):\n   - `db.malware.remove({})`\n8. **Verify count is zero**:\n   - `db.malware.find().count()`\n9. Exit MongoDB:\n   - `exit`\n\n## Notes / alternatives (if you don’t want to delete everything)\n- **Delete by time window (Unix time in milliseconds):**\n  - Count: `db.malware.find({\"timestamp\":{$lt:<end>, $gte:<start>}}).count()`\n  - Remove: `db.malware.remove({\"timestamp\":{$lt:<end>, $gte:<start>}})`\n- **Delete by malware name (example):**\n  - Count: `db.malware.find({\"name\":\"test.exe\"}).pretty().count()`\n  - Remove: `db.malware.remove({\"name\":\"test.exe\"})`\n\nThe KB content describes deleting alerts from the database; it doesn’t describe a UI-only “bulk clear” action specifically for “Needs your attention.”\n\nSources:\n- Article #000023683: \"Delete Malware Alerts in Bulk\" (v1, updated 2025-11-14T16:29:20.000+0000)\n- Article #000016846: \"Manage Malware Alerts\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T21:12:53.000+0000)\n- Article #000021118: \"How to Delete all Malware Alerts\" (v3, updated 2025-12-01T21:23:20.000+0000)",

      "actual_answer": "You can check when MalOp data was exported to DI on the **Detection Server(s)** by reviewing the **VC exporter audit log**.\n\n- **Where to look**\n  - On each Detection Server:  \n    `/opt/cybereason/logs/vc-export-audit.log`\n\n- **How to generate/refresh the export entries (so they appear in the log)**\n  - SSH to the Detection Server and run:\n    - `curl -kL https://localhost:18443/transparency/rest/vc/exporter/exportAll/MalopDetectionEvents`\n    - `curl -kL https://localhost:18443/transparency/rest/vc/exporter/exportAll/MalopProcess`\n\n- **How to find the MalOp export entries**\n  - Filter the audit log for the MalOp element types:\n    - `grep -i \"MalopDetectionEvents\" /opt/cybereason/logs/vc-export-audit.log`\n    - `grep -i \"MalopProcess\" /opt/cybereason/logs/vc-export-audit.log`\n\nWhat I found in the KB is that exports are recorded in `vc-export-audit.log` and can be filtered by `MalopDetectionEvents` / `MalopProcess`.       "ground_truth": "Incorrect password failures show as Login|6 with cn1=0 (actionSuccess=0). Successful logins show as Login|0 with cn1=1 (actionSuccess=1).",
      "actual_answer": "In `userAuditSyslog.log`, the login result is indicated by the event code in the CEF “name” field and by `cn1Label=actionSuccess cn1=<value>`:\n\n- **Bad password login (failure)**\n  - Look for `UserAction|General/Login|6|` **and/or**\n  - `cn1Label=actionSuccess cn1=0`\n  - Example pattern: `...|General/Login|6|... cn1Label=actionSuccess cn1=0 ... cs2Label=loginMethod cs2=PASSWORD ...`\n\n- **Successful login**\n  - Look for `UserAction|General/Login|0|` **and**\n  - `cn1Label=actionSuccess cn1=1`\n  - Example pattern: `...|General/Login|0|... cn1Label=actionSuccess cn1=1 ... cs2Label=loginMethod cs2=PASSWORD ...`\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021202: \"How to Investigate Password Login Failure Issues from a Syslog File\" (v2, updated 2025-12-08T21:04:11.000+0000)\n- Article #000022910: \"Create a User\" (v4, updated 2025-10-31T15:22:19.000+0000)\n- Article #000022911: \"Delete a User\" (v3, updated 2025-10-31T15:29:34.000+0000)\n- Article #000021312: \"Empty Username in User Audit Log\" (v2, updated 2026-01-12T19:37:41.000+0000)\n- Article #000022212: \"Server Logs\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T19:44:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000014950: \"Download Audit Logs\" (v2, updated 2025-09-19T22:21:16.000+0000)",

      "query": "How do I restore hidden sensor installer zips back so they show in UI again?",
      "ground_truth": "On the detection server, move the ZIPs from the hidden folder back to /opt/cybereason/installation-packages/versions/, then remove the hidden directory.",
      "actual_answer": "To make hidden sensor installer `.zip` packages show in the UI again, move them back from the `hidden` folder to the main `versions` directory on the Detection Server(s), then remove the `hidden` folder.\n\n- On the Detection Server(s), run:\n  1. `cd /opt/cybereason/installation-packages/versions/hidden`\n  2. `mv *.zip /opt/cybereason/installation-packages/versions/`\n  3. `cd ..`\n  4. `rmdir hidden`\n\nAfter this, the installers should appear again in the UI under **Sensors > Overview > Download Cybereason Installers**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021130: \"How to Hide Sensor Package Installers from the UI\" (v2, updated 2025-12-08T19:52:32.000+0000)\n- Article #000021541: \"Sensor is not Displayed in the Sensors Screen\" (v3, updated 2025-12-03T21:10:48.000+0000)\n- Article #000022967: \"Restore a Removed Sensor\" (v3, updated 2025-10-31T19:24:30.000+0000)\n- Article #000021445: \"A Newly Installed Endpoint Sensor Does not Appear in the Cybereason UI\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T18:13:25.000+0000)\n- Article #000021462: \"Last Update Status showing as Failed although Sensor Upgrade was Successful\" (v4, updated 2025-12-03T19:38:41.000+0000)",

      "query_id": "tc_0658",
      "query": "Default queue lifetime for actions sent to offline sensors?",
      "ground_truth": "Offline sensor actions are queued for 3 days by default. If the sensor stays offline past that, the action won’t run later.",
      "actual_answer": "The default queue lifetime for actions sent to **offline sensors is 3 days**.\n\n- If the sensor comes back online within those 3 days, the action executes.\n- If the sensor is still offline after 3 days, the action is no longer queued and **will not execute** even if the sensor comes online later.\n- You can **customize** this default queue period by contacting **Cybereason Technical Support**.\n\nSources:\n- Article #000021927: \"Supported Capabilities for Offline Sensors\" (v2, updated 2025-06-20T21:03:26.000+0000)\n- Article #000021005: \"Configure the Timeout of Primed Actions for Offline Sensors\" (v4, updated 2025-12-08T18:12:41.000+0000)\n- Article #000016793: \"Monitor and Manage Sensors\" (v4, updated 2025-11-24T20:50:14.000+0000)\n- Article #000023113: \"21.2 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-13T19:59:31.000+0000)\n- Article #000023130: \"21.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-13T16:51:08.000+0000)\n- Article #000023127: \"22.1 All Versions\" (v5, updated 2025-11-14T18:42:18.000+0000)",
